practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the mental health continuum?
A) A fixed category dividing people into mentally ill or mentally healthy
B) A scale from mentally healthy to severely mentally unwell, along which a person's position can change
C) A list of official diagnoses recognised by the ICD
D) A policy of caring for patients only within hospitals
practice_questions.marks: B) A scale from mentally healthy to severely mentally unwell, along which a person's position can change [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'prevalence' in relation to mental health, giving an example statistic from your lesson.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering/Secure: Correct definition of prevalence (how common a condition is in a population) plus an accurate example statistic (e.g. one in ten young people). [2 marks]
Developing: Definition given but example missing or inaccurate. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague or incorrect description. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: A college has 600 students. Using the statistic that one in ten young people experience a mental health problem, calculate how many students at the college would be expected to experience a mental health problem. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering/Secure: Working shown (600 \div 10) and correct answer of 60 students. [2 marks]
Developing: Correct method but arithmetic error, or correct answer with no working shown. [1 mark]
Emerging: Incorrect method and incorrect answer. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how attitudes towards mental health in the UK have changed since the 1959 Mental Health Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of the shift from compulsory, long-term institutional admission before 1959 to informal admission, community-based care, and modern anti-stigma campaigns, with detail. [3 marks]
Secure: Accurate description covering at least two of these points. [2 marks]
Developing: Basic, undeveloped point about attitudes changing. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague or irrelevant answer. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the reported incidence of mental health problems has increased over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two reasons (e.g. increased recognition of symptoms; lessening of social stigma) each explained with a clear link to why this raises reported figures. [4 marks]
Secure: Two reasons identified with at least partial explanation, or one reason fully explained. [2-3 marks]
Developing: Reasons named with little or no explanation. [1 mark]
Emerging: No relevant reasons given. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: A newspaper article describes a man who was afraid to tell his employer about his diagnosis of depression in case he lost his job, but who later told close friends who were supportive. Using this source, apply your knowledge of stigma and discrimination to explain the man's experience before and after disclosing his diagnosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Applies stigma to explain the man's fear before disclosure and links discrimination to the risk of job loss; explains how disclosure to friends shows a reduction in stigma's effect after diagnosis, all explicitly tied to the source. [4-5 marks]
Secure: Identifies stigma and discrimination correctly with some application to the source. [3 marks]
Developing: Names stigma or discrimination with limited application to the source. [1-2 marks]
Emerging: No relevant application. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is not one of the three functions of sleep identified in the specification?
A) A healthy brain
B) Physical repair
C) Emotional stability
D) Increased muscle mass
practice_questions.marks: D) Increased muscle mass is correct, as this is not one of the three named functions of sleep (healthy brain, physical repair, emotional stability). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the hormone released by the pineal gland that regulates the sleep-wake cycle.
practice_questions.marks: Melatonin. [1 mark for correct term]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by an exogenous zeitgeber.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: An external cue that resets or influences the body's internal clock.
1 mark: A correct example given, such as daylight, darkness or meal times.
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A sleep researcher recorded the number of hours slept by five participants in one night: 6, 7, 5, 8 and 9 hours. Calculate the mean number of hours slept, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: (6 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 9) ÷ 5 = 35 ÷ 5 [1 mark]
Answer: 7 hours [1 mark]
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between sleep onset insomnia and sleep maintenance insomnia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly describes both forms of insomnia with accurate detail — sleep onset insomnia as difficulty falling asleep, sleep maintenance insomnia as difficulty staying asleep, with an appropriate cause or example for each.
Secure: Describes both forms correctly but with less detail or no example.
Developing: Describes one form of insomnia accurately, or confuses onset and maintenance.
Emerging: Vague or inaccurate reference to insomnia with little relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how exogenous zeitgebers can disrupt a person's sleep-wake cycle. Use an example such as shift work or travelling across time zones in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains clearly how exogenous zeitgebers (e.g. light, darkness) normally keep the endogenous pacemaker on schedule, and explains how a specific example (shift work/time zone travel) creates a mismatch that disrupts sleep, using correct terminology throughout.
Secure: Explains the general link between disrupted zeitgebers and sleep problems, with a relevant example, but the explanation of the mismatch is less developed.
Developing: Names a relevant example and states that it disrupts sleep, but does not explain why in terms of pacemakers or zeitgebers.
Emerging: Limited or inaccurate reference to sleep disruption with no clear example.

practice_questions.text:
Which stage of development covers the period from conception to birth?
A) Childhood
B) Adolescence
C) Pre-natal
D) Adulthood
practice_questions.marks: C) Pre-natal [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the brain structure responsible for controlling automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate.
practice_questions.marks: Brain stem [1 mark]. No credit for 'brain' alone.

practice_questions.text: Outline what happens to synapses that are rarely used during brain development.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that unused synapses weaken/are pruned away; 1 mark for contrasting this with frequently used connections being strengthened.

practice_questions.text: Five students complete an IQ test, scoring 95, 105, 110, 100 and 90. Calculate the mean IQ score for the group. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct total (95+105+110+100+90 = 500); 1 mark for correct division (500 ÷ 5 = 100). Answer: 100. Full marks require working shown.

practice_questions.text: Describe how brain development follows a bottom-up sequence, referring to two named brain structures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names two structures in correct developmental order with accurate, specific functions.
Secure: Names two structures with broadly accurate functions but order not made explicit.
Developing: Names one structure correctly, or confuses the order of maturation.
Emerging: Vague reference to 'brain parts' with no named structures.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the cortex being the last brain structure to mature is significant for learning during childhood and adolescence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the cortex's late, prolonged maturation means it remains open to being shaped by experience, directly linking this to ongoing improvements in reasoning, language and problem-solving through adolescence.
Secure: States that the cortex matures late and links this generally to learning and cognitive skill.
Developing: Describes the cortex's function without explaining why late maturation matters for learning.
Emerging: States only that the cortex is 'for thinking' with no development.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes obedience?
A) Changing your opinion to match a group of friends
B) Following the direct instruction of a person in a position of authority
C) Acting differently because you are part of a large crowd
D) Refusing to follow any instructions from other people
practice_questions.marks: B) Following the direct instruction of a person in a position of authority [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of anti-social behaviour that can occur within a crowd.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any appropriate example, such as: rioting; looting; vandalism; violence towards others in a crowd situation. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what psychologists mean by 'majority influence'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that majority influence is when the larger group affects the beliefs or behaviour of an individual or minority; 1 further mark for development, e.g. that this can happen through social pressure to fit in, without a direct order. [2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between pro-social and anti-social crowd behaviour. Use one example of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear, accurate distinction with a well-chosen example of both pro-social and anti-social behaviour (e.g. crowd raising charity donations vs crowd rioting). Secure: Accurate distinction with at least one relevant example. Developing: Basic distinction made but examples are vague or only one type is covered. Emerging: Simple or partially correct statement with no clear example.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a person might obey the instructions of an authority figure, even if they personally disagree with the instruction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed explanatory points showing clear links between cause and effect (e.g. the person recognises the authority figure's legitimate position and fears the consequences of disobedience), using accurate psychological terminology. Secure: Two points made with some explanation, though development may be limited. Developing: One explained point, or two points that are mostly descriptive rather than explanatory. Emerging: A simple, undeveloped point about following orders.

practice_questions.text: A local council introduces new recycling bins on every street. At first, only a few residents use them. Within two months, most residents on the street are recycling regularly, even though many did not support the scheme when it began. Using your knowledge of majority influence, explain how this change in behaviour might have occurred.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clearly applies majority influence to the source, explaining that as more residents began recycling, the growing majority created social pressure on the remaining residents to conform, with accurate use of terminology throughout. Secure: Applies majority influence to the source with reasonable accuracy, though the explanation may be less detailed. Developing: Makes a general point about people copying others, with limited explicit reference to the source. Emerging: Describes majority influence in general terms only, without applying it to the scenario.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a null hypothesis for a study into noise and concentration?
A) Participants who complete a test in a noisy room will make significantly more errors than participants in a silent room.
B) There will be no significant difference in the number of errors made between participants tested in a noisy room and those tested in a silent room; any difference is due to chance.
C) There is a correlation between noise level and number of errors made.
D) Noise makes people worse at concentrating.
practice_questions.marks: B) is correct. It predicts no difference and states that any difference found is due to chance, which defines a null hypothesis. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A researcher tests whether drinking coffee before an exam improves test scores. Identify the independent variable in this study.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for correctly identifying: whether or not participants drink coffee before the exam (presence/absence, or amount, of coffee). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by a correlational hypothesis, using an example involving two co-variables.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for stating that a correlational hypothesis predicts a relationship or association between two co-variables, not cause and effect.
1 mark for a suitable example, e.g. 'there is a positive correlation between hours of sleep and exam score.'
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A researcher is investigating whether background music affects memory recall in a word-list task. Describe how the researcher could use standardisation to control extraneous variables in this study.
practice_questions.marks:
• Identifies a relevant extraneous variable, e.g. room, word list difficulty, time of day (1)
• States that standardisation means keeping the procedure identical for every participant except the IV condition (1)
• Gives a specific applied example, e.g. using the same word list, same room and same instructions for all participants (1)
[3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using a repeated measures design rather than an independent measures design in an experiment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both a strength and a weakness are explained with clear, developed links to repeated measures design, using correct terminology such as participant variables and order effects.
Secure: Both a strength and a weakness are identified with some explanation.
Developing: One point is identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped point(s) only.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A psychologist wants to find out if listening to classical music improves problem-solving ability. Twenty participants are randomly allocated to two groups. Group A listens to classical music for 10 minutes then completes a puzzle. Group B sits in silence for 10 minutes then completes the same puzzle. The psychologist records how many puzzle pieces each participant places correctly in 5 minutes.

Using the source above, identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and the experimental design used. Explain one extraneous variable the psychologist should control.
practice_questions.marks:
• IV correctly identified: whether participants listen to classical music or sit in silence (1)
• DV correctly identified: number of puzzle pieces placed correctly in 5 minutes (1)
• Design correctly identified: independent measures design, as different participants are used in each group (1)
• A relevant extraneous variable is named, e.g. prior experience with puzzles, time of day (1)
• Explanation of how this variable could affect the DV if not controlled (1)
[5 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following shows the correct order of the five stages of information processing in memory?
A) Encoding, input, storage, retrieval, output
B) Input, encoding, storage, retrieval, output
C) Storage, retrieval, encoding, input, output
D) Output, retrieval, storage, encoding, input
practice_questions.marks: B) Input, encoding, storage, retrieval, output [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by displacement as a type of forgetting.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that a memory store has limited capacity; one further mark for explaining that new information entering the store pushes out and replaces older information, which is then lost. [2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: In a memory experiment, 25 participants were shown a list of 16 words. On average, participants correctly recalled 12 of the words after a short delay. Calculate the percentage of words correctly recalled on average, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for correct method (12 ÷ 16 × 100); one mark for the correct answer of 75%, given to an appropriate number of significant figures. [2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe how damage to the hippocampus can affect a person's memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names anterograde amnesia and gives a developed, accurate description linking hippocampal damage to the inability to form new long-term memories, while noting older memories can remain intact.
Secure: Names anterograde amnesia and describes the main effect (inability to form new long-term memories after damage).
Developing: States that hippocampal damage affects memory but description is vague or only partly accurate.
Emerging: Simple or incomplete point with little accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how retrieval failure due to a lack of cues can cause a person to forget information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives a fully developed explanation showing that information is stored but inaccessible without a matching retrieval cue, with a clear cause-and-effect link and appropriate terminology throughout.
Secure: Explains that a missing cue prevents access to a stored memory, with reasonable development of the point.
Developing: Describes retrieval failure without clearly explaining why the missing cue causes forgetting.
Emerging: Basic or inaccurate reference to forgetting with little explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Read the source, then answer the question that follows.

Source: Amara suffered a head injury that damaged her hippocampus. Since the injury, she can still remember her childhood holidays clearly, but she cannot remember meeting new people she was introduced to yesterday, and she has to be reminded every day about her new daily routine.

Using the source, explain how Amara's memory problems relate to anterograde amnesia and the role of the hippocampus.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Applies the term anterograde amnesia accurately to Amara's inability to form new long-term memories, links this explicitly to hippocampal damage, and uses specific detail from the source (e.g. remembering childhood holidays but not new people) to support the explanation.
Secure: Identifies anterograde amnesia and the hippocampus and makes a reasonable link to the source, with some specific detail used.
Developing: Identifies relevant terms (amnesia/hippocampus) but link to the source is limited or generic.
Emerging: Minimal reference to the source; description of memory problems without applying psychological terms.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher wants to select participants using a method that gives every member of a school equal chance of being chosen. Which sampling method is this?
A) Opportunity sampling
B) Self-selected sampling
C) Random sampling
D) Volunteer sampling
practice_questions.marks: C) Random sampling [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A researcher tells participants they are taking part in a maths test, but is secretly measuring their stress levels without telling them beforehand. Identify the ethical issue raised by this study.
practice_questions.marks: Deception (participants were not told the true purpose of the study). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by self-selected sampling.
practice_questions.marks: Participants volunteer to take part themselves rather than being chosen by the researcher [1 mark]; for example, by responding to an advert or a request for participants [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A target population contains 400 students. A researcher uses random sampling to select 40 students to take part in her study. What percentage of the target population is included in the sample? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 40 ÷ 400 = 0.1 [1 mark]; 0.1 × 100 = 10% [1 mark]. Correct method shown earns credit even if the final answer contains an arithmetic error. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A researcher plans to study children's reactions to a stressful classroom task without telling their parents beforehand. Explain two ethical issues raised by this study and how the researcher could deal with each one.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both issues (lack of informed consent; protection of participants from psychological harm) clearly explained with a developed, matched solution for each — for example, obtaining parental or guardian consent in advance, and offering debriefing and support afterwards — using accurate psychological terminology throughout.
Secure: Two relevant ethical issues identified with an appropriate solution for each, though explanation may be less developed.
Developing: One ethical issue identified and explained, or two issues named with limited explanation of solutions.
Emerging: Simple identification of an ethical issue with little or no explanation of a solution.

practice_questions.text: Source: A psychology student stood outside her college canteen and asked whichever students walked past whether they would fill in a short survey about sleep habits. She did not check whether her final sample matched the age and gender mix of the whole college. Using the source, identify the sampling method used and evaluate one strength and one weakness of this method as applied in this study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies opportunity sampling from the source, with a strength and weakness explicitly linked to details in the source (e.g. quick to carry out near the canteen; likely biased towards students who happen to eat there at that time, so may not represent the whole college).
Secure: Correctly identifies opportunity sampling with a relevant strength and weakness, with some reference to the source.
Developing: Correctly identifies the sampling method with limited application to the source.
Emerging: Attempts to name a sampling method with little or no development.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'accommodation' in Piaget's theory?
A) Fitting new information into an existing schema without changing it
B) Changing or creating a schema because new information does not fit
C) Understanding that quantity stays the same despite appearance changing
D) Believing an inanimate object has feelings
practice_questions.marks: B) Changing or creating a schema because new information does not fit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'object permanence'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight; 1 mark for linking this to the sensori-motor stage or a relevant example (e.g. searching for a hidden toy). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens when a pre-operational child is tested on Piaget's conservation of number task.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear description of two equal rows being shown, one row spread out with no counters added/removed, and the child incorrectly judging the longer row to have more. Secure: Most of this described with minor gaps. Developing: Basic description of the counters task without the key outcome. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate reference to the study.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a concrete-operational child, but not a pre-operational child, can correctly solve a conservation of number task.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that the concrete-operational child has developed decentration (can consider more than the row's length) and reversibility (can mentally undo the transformation), so recognises the number is unchanged; pre-operational child lacks both and focuses only on visual length. Secure: Explains one of decentration or reversibility clearly linked to conservation. Developing: States the child 'understands more' without explaining why. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text: A four-year-old is shown two rows of buttons that she agrees have the same number. She watches an adult spread one row out and then says that row now has more buttons. When her older brother eats the last biscuit, she insists he must be sad because 'the plate is sad it's empty.' Using this source, identify and explain two features of Piaget's pre-operational stage shown by the girl's behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies lack of conservation (judging number by row length rather than logic) and animism (attributing feelings to the plate), explaining each clearly with direct reference to the source. Secure: Identifies both features with some reference to the source. Developing: Identifies one feature correctly, limited explanation. Emerging: Vague identification without linking to the source.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development, including reference to the reductionism/holism debate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced essay describing the four stages and assimilation/accommodation, then evaluating using the reductionism/holism debate (e.g. the conservation of number task reduces a child's understanding to one narrow response versus a holistic view based on real-world number use), each point elaborated with a reason, reaching a clear supported judgement. Secure: Clear description and evaluation with at least one developed point on reductionism/holism, sustained argument. Developing: Some description, limited or undeveloped evaluation, no clear judgement. Emerging: Largely descriptive with minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which situational factor did Bickman's (1974) study investigate?
A) Majority influence on conformity
B) The effect of a uniform on obedience
C) Culture and anti-social behaviour
D) Deindividuation in crowds
practice_questions.marks: B) The effect of a uniform on obedience [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one way a crowd can affect an individual's behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: deindividuation / loss of personal identity; reduced sense of personal responsibility; increased anonymity leading to anti-social or pro-social behaviour. [1 mark for any one correct point]

practice_questions.text: Describe how deindividuation can lead to anti-social behaviour in a crowd.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly describes anonymity reducing personal responsibility and links this directly to a specific example of anti-social behaviour (e.g. looting, vandalism).
Secure: Describes the loss of personal identity/responsibility in a crowd and links it to anti-social behaviour, with some detail.
Developing: Makes a basic point about crowds and behaviour change but explanation of deindividuation is limited or vague.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped statement about crowds; no clear description of deindividuation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Bickman's (1974) study supports a situational, rather than dispositional, explanation of obedience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that obedience was highest in the guard uniform condition, showing the visual symbol of authority alone increased compliance, and links this explicitly to situational (not personality-based) causes.
Secure: Explains that the uniform increased obedience compared with civilian clothing, with a clear link to situational influence.
Developing: States that the study found different obedience levels for different outfits but explanation of why this supports a situational view is limited.
Emerging: Basic or inaccurate reference to the study; little explanation of situational versus dispositional causes.

practice_questions.text: A local council wants to test whether pedestrians are more likely to follow a diversion sign held up by a person wearing a high-visibility council uniform, compared with the same instruction given by a person in ordinary clothes. Using your knowledge of situational factors and Bickman's (1974) study, explain how this investigation relates to research into authority and obedience, and suggest one way the researcher could improve the reliability of the results.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Applies the concept of legitimate authority and Bickman's uniform findings explicitly to the council scenario, and suggests a specific, workable improvement to reliability (e.g. standardising the instruction given, repeating across multiple locations/times).
Secure: Links the scenario clearly to situational factors and Bickman's study, with a relevant but less developed improvement.
Developing: Makes a general link between the scenario and obedience/uniforms but application is limited; improvement suggested is vague.
Emerging: Minimal or no application to the specific scenario; no clear improvement offered.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that situational factors, rather than personality, provide the best explanation for why people conform, obey and behave differently in crowds. Refer to Bickman's (1974) study and the free will/determinism debate in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument drawing on majority influence, deindividuation, culture and authority (including Bickman's findings), with sustained evaluation (e.g. the free will/determinism debate, individual differences in response to the same situation) and a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Clear argument covering more than one situational factor with relevant evidence (e.g. Bickman) and explained evaluation points, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Some description of situational factors with limited evaluation; judgement may be asserted rather than justified.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about conformity or obedience; little or no evaluation or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes a child adopting the attitudes and behaviour of an admired role model as their own?
A) Imitation
B) Identification
C) Vicarious reinforcement
D) Internalisation
practice_questions.marks: B) Identification [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the psychologists who carried out the 1986 study into video games and aggression in children.
practice_questions.marks: Cooper and Mackie [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: In a class re-creation of Cooper and Mackie's study, five children who played the aggressive video game were given aggression ratings of 6, 8, 5, 9 and 7 by an observer. Calculate the mean aggression rating for this group. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for correct method shown (6+8+5+9+7 = 35, then 35 divided by 5)
1 mark for correct answer (mean = 7)

practice_questions.text: Explain how vicarious reinforcement can lead a child to imitate criminal behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A fully developed explanation with a clear causal chain linking observation of a rewarded role model to vicarious learning and imitation, using accurate psychological terminology throughout.
Secure: A clear explanation of vicarious reinforcement with some development of cause and effect.
Developing: A basic or partially explained point about reinforcement or imitation, with limited development.
Emerging: A vague or inaccurate reference to learning from others, with little clear explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Read the source and answer the question that follows.

Source: Jamal is fourteen. His older brother Tyrell has been arrested twice for shoplifting, and each time he has come home laughing and shown Jamal the goods, including a new phone he says he 'got for free'. Jamal has started shoplifting from the same shops as his brother.

Apply Social Learning Theory to explain why Jamal has started shoplifting.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names and applies at least two Social Learning Theory processes (e.g. identification with Tyrell as a same-sex, older role model; vicarious reinforcement from seeing Tyrell rewarded with the phone) explicitly to details in the source, using accurate terminology.
Secure: Names and applies at least one Social Learning Theory process clearly to a detail in the source.
Developing: Refers to Social Learning Theory in general terms with only a weak or implicit link to the source.
Emerging: General comments about crime with little or no reference to the theory or the source.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the Social Learning Theory of Criminality as an explanation of why people commit crime. In your answer, refer to research evidence and the nature/nurture debate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, balanced line of reasoning that explains the theory's key processes (identification, observation/imitation, reinforcement, internalisation), uses Cooper and Mackie (1986) as developed supporting evidence, evaluates the theory with well-developed points (e.g. ecological validity of lab studies, the nature/nurture debate, individual differences in who imitates role models), and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Explains most processes of the theory accurately, refers to Cooper and Mackie's study as evidence, and includes at least two developed evaluative points, reaching a judgement that is not always fully justified.
Developing: Describes the theory with some accuracy but evaluation is limited to brief, undeveloped points; the study may be mentioned but not linked clearly to evaluation; no clear final judgement.
Emerging: Basic or muddled description of the theory with little or no evaluation and no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which term best describes unfair treatment of a person because of a mental health diagnosis, such as being refused a job?
A) Stigma
B) Discrimination
C) Self-stigma
D) Care in the community
practice_questions.marks: B) Discrimination [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why stigma might stop a person seeking help before they receive a diagnosis.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any one of the following:
• Fear of being judged or labelled
• Worry about being seen as 'weak' or 'dangerous'
• Concern about how family or friends will react
[1 mark for any one correct reason]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'care in the community' as a response to mental health problems.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying the idea (supporting people to live in their own home/community rather than a psychiatric hospital) plus one further mark for development (e.g. with support from community mental health teams, GPs or social workers).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two effects that discrimination can have on a person after they have received a diagnosis of a mental health problem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two effects explained in detail with clear links to how discrimination changes the person's life (e.g. job loss reducing income and self-worth; social exclusion increasing isolation), using accurate psychological vocabulary.
Secure: Two effects identified and explained with some development, such as unfair treatment at work or exclusion from social activities.
Developing: One or two effects identified with limited explanation of how they impact the person.
Emerging: Effects named with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Amir was diagnosed with clinical depression last year. Since then, his manager has quietly reduced his responsibilities at work without discussing it with him, and Amir has stopped telling new colleagues about his diagnosis because he worries they will treat him differently.

Using the information about Amir, apply your knowledge of the effects of mental health problems to explain two ways his diagnosis appears to have affected him.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both stigma/discrimination-related effects (e.g. discrimination at work through reduced responsibilities; self-stigma or fear of others' reactions leading to concealment) clearly identified and explicitly linked to details in Amir's case.
Secure: Two relevant effects identified with some reference to Amir's situation, though links may be less developed.
Developing: One effect identified and linked to the source, or two effects given with only generic reference to the source.
Emerging: General knowledge of stigma/discrimination given with little or no application to Amir's situation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that discrimination after a diagnosis causes more harm to a person than stigma before diagnosis. Use your knowledge of the effects of mental health problems on individuals and on wider society to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, balanced argument that explains and evaluates effects of stigma before diagnosis (e.g. delayed help-seeking) against effects of discrimination after diagnosis (e.g. job loss, exclusion, self-stigma), draws on wider societal effects such as care in the community, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: A generally balanced answer covering both before and after diagnosis with some evaluation, reaching a judgement that is partly supported.
Developing: Mostly descriptive answer covering one side (before or after) in more depth than the other, with limited evaluation or a weak/unsupported judgement.
Emerging: Brief or one-sided answer with little evaluation and no clear judgement.

before.exam_tip_html: Keep stigma (an attitude) and discrimination (an action) clearly separate in your answers, and always say whether you are describing an effect before or after diagnosis — examiners reward this precision. For ‘Apply to a Source’ questions, name the concept (e.g. discrimination, self-stigma) and then explicitly point to the detail in the scenario that shows it — don’t just repeat generic textbook knowledge. For the 13-mark essay, spend real time on evaluation: for every point you describe, add a developed reason for or against it, and finish with a clear judgement rather than trailing off.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the capacity of short-term memory?
A) Around 3 items
B) Around 7 items, plus or minus 2
C) Completely unlimited
D) Around 20 items
practice_questions.marks: B) Around 7 items, plus or minus 2 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the memory store in the multi-store model that has a potentially unlimited capacity and can last a lifetime.
practice_questions.marks: Long-term memory (LTM) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline how information is coded when it first enters the sensory register.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that coding matches the sense used (e.g. visual or acoustic); 1 further mark for naming or explaining an example, such as iconic (visual) or echoic (auditory) memory. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Four participants recall the following number of words after a short-term memory test: 6, 8, 7, 7. Calculate the mean number of words recalled. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working (6+8+7+7 = 28, divided by 4); 1 mark for the correct answer of 7 words. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Wilson, Kopelman and Kapur (2008) case study of Clive Wearing supports the idea that long-term memory is not a single, unitary store.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains clearly that Clive Wearing's hippocampal damage disrupted his episodic memory (he could not form new lasting memories) while his procedural memory, such as playing the piano, remained intact, and links this directly to different types of LTM depending on different brain structures.
Secure: Explains that Clive Wearing lost some types of memory but kept others, linking this to different memory stores or brain areas, with minor gaps.
Developing: Describes what happened to Clive Wearing but gives limited explanation of why this challenges a single unitary long-term memory store.
Emerging: Basic or partial reference to the case study with little explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Read the source and answer the question that follows.

Source: Amira was in a car accident and suffered a head injury. Doctors found that the front part of her brain was damaged. Since the accident, Amira struggles to recall details from the weeks leading up to the crash, although she can still learn and remember new information from day to day.

Using your knowledge of the multi-store model and the brain, explain which type of amnesia Amira is most likely experiencing and why.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies retrograde amnesia and links it explicitly to the frontal lobe damage described in the source, explaining that Amira's difficulty is recalling memories from before the injury while her ability to form new memories is unaffected, using detail from the source throughout.
Secure: Identifies retrograde amnesia and gives a reasonable brain-based explanation, referring to some detail from the source.
Developing: Identifies a general type of amnesia or brain link with limited reference to the source.
Emerging: Vague or unsupported answer with little use of the source.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the manifest content of a dream?
A) The repressed wish hidden underneath the dream
B) The actual images and events the dreamer remembers
C) The stage of sleep in which dreaming occurs
D) The brain activity recorded during REM sleep
practice_questions.marks: B) The actual images and events the dreamer remembers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the term Freud used for the true, hidden meaning of a dream.
practice_questions.marks: Latent content. [1 mark for correct term]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by repression in Freud's theory of dreaming.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying repression as pushing distressing thoughts/desires out of conscious awareness; 1 further mark for linking this to the material staying active in the unconscious mind. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how wish fulfilment can lead to disguised imagery appearing in dreams.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed, logical chain of reasoning linking repression, the unconscious mind, and disguise/symbolism, using accurate terminology throughout.
Secure: A clear explanation covering most of the causal chain (repressed wish cannot be expressed directly, so appears disguised) with mostly accurate terminology.
Developing: Basic explanation identifying wish fulfilment or repression but with limited development of how/why disguise occurs.
Emerging: A simple, undeveloped statement with little or no explanatory link.

practice_questions.text: A student describes a recurring dream in which she is constantly late for an important exam and cannot find the exam room. Using Freud's theory, suggest what the manifest content of this dream might be, and what latent content it could be disguising.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly identifies the manifest content from the source (being late, unable to find the room) and offers a plausible, well-linked latent content (e.g. a repressed anxiety about failure or losing control), explicitly applying Freud's terms to the scenario.
Secure: Identifies manifest content accurately and suggests a reasonable latent content, with some clear application to the source.
Developing: Identifies manifest content but latent content is vague, generic or only loosely linked to the source.
Emerging: Minimal or no clear application of manifest/latent content to the given source.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Freud's theory of dreaming, using evidence from the Wolfman study (Freud, 1918) to support your judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, balanced argument that explains the theory (unconscious mind, repression, wish fulfilment, manifest/latent content), uses the Wolfman study as developed supporting evidence, and evaluates using elaborated points (e.g. subjectivity, generalisability, unfalsifiability) each with a clear reason, reaching a supported overall judgement.
Secure: A clear explanation of the theory with relevant use of the Wolfman study and at least two developed evaluation points, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Some accurate description of the theory and study with limited or undeveloped evaluation; judgement may be weak or missing.
Emerging: Basic, list-like points with little explanation or evaluation and no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes the belief that intelligence is a fixed trait that effort cannot change?
A) Growth mindset
B) Fixed mindset
C) Self-efficacy
D) Verbaliser
practice_questions.marks: B) Fixed mindset [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A class replicates the intervention stage of Blackwell et al. (2007). The growth-mindset group (20 students) has a mean maths score of 68. The control group (20 students) has a mean maths score of 60. Calculate the difference between the two means and state which group scored higher. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
68 − 60 = 8 [1 mark for correct calculation with working shown]
Growth-mindset group scored higher [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the method used in the Blackwell et al. (2007) study into fixed and growth mindsets.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurately describes the longitudinal design tracking mindset and maths grades, the intervention comparing a growth-mindset workshop group against a control group taught about memory, and the sample of students transitioning to secondary school.
Secure: Describes most of the design, sample and procedure with minor gaps or imprecise terminology.
Developing: Gives one or two accurate points about the study's method without full detail.
Emerging: Vague or minimal reference to the study.

practice_questions.text: Explain Willingham's criticism of learning styles theory, referring to his idea about the importance of meaning in learning.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that preference for a style does not equal effectiveness, that content should determine format (e.g. visual for spatial information, verbal for arguments), and links this clearly to Willingham's point that meaning, not style, drives learning, with a developed example.
Secure: Explains at least two of these points with some development and correct terminology.
Developing: States one relevant point about learning styles or meaning without much explanation.
Emerging: Simple or unclear reference to learning styles.

practice_questions.text: Priya says: 'I always get top marks in art but I'm rubbish at maths, and I always will be — there's no point trying harder.' Using your knowledge of Dweck's Mindset Theory, identify which mindset Priya is showing and suggest one change to how she could think about her maths ability.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies Priya's fixed mindset with clear reference to the source ('always will be', 'no point trying'), and gives a well-developed, plausible growth-mindset reframe (e.g. focusing on effort and strategy rather than fixed ability) linked back to the source.
Secure: Identifies the fixed mindset with reference to the source and gives a relevant but less developed suggestion for change.
Developing: Identifies the mindset with limited link to the source, or gives a suggestion without identifying the mindset clearly.
Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate application to the source.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that a person's mindset is the main factor that determines how well they learn. Draw on Dweck's Mindset Theory, Willingham's ideas about learning, and the nature/nurture debate in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, sustained argument drawing on Dweck's theory (including the Blackwell et al. findings), Willingham's emphasis on meaning over style, and the nature/nurture debate; each evaluation point is elaborated with a reason; reaches a clear, well-supported judgement.
Secure: Clear argument covering most of Dweck, Willingham and the nature/nurture debate with relevant evidence and some elaborated evaluation; judgement present but less fully supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge of mindset and/or learning styles with basic evaluation; judgement is weak or unclear; description outweighs evaluation.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about mindset or learning styles; little or no evaluation or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which brain region is most associated with auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia, due to its role in processing sound and language?
A) Frontal lobes
B) Cerebellum
C) Temporal lobes
D) Hippocampus
practice_questions.marks: C) Temporal lobes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the neurotransmitter that the dopamine hypothesis states is present in abnormally high levels in the brains of people with schizophrenia.
practice_questions.marks: Dopamine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the 'social drift theory' of schizophrenia.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: People with schizophrenia move down the social scale over time (rather than social class causing the disorder).
1 mark: This happens through rejection by society and/or disengagement of the individual.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an overactive dopamine system could lead to the positive symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hallucinations and delusions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear chain of explanation linking dopaminergic neuron activity, through excess synaptic transmission, to specific positive symptoms, using accurate specialist vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Explains that excess dopamine at synapses overstimulates neural pathways, with some link made to symptoms.
Developing: Describes the dopamine hypothesis but does not clearly explain the causal link to symptoms.
Emerging: Basic or vague reference to dopamine without explanation of how it causes symptoms.

practice_questions.text: Read the source: Amir has been diagnosed with schizophrenia. After his employer heard about the diagnosis, Amir was excluded from team meetings and eventually let go from his job. Since then, Amir has moved to a smaller flat in a poorer part of the city and rarely leaves the house. Using the social drift theory, explain what has happened to Amir.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and applies both rejection (exclusion, job loss) and disengagement (withdrawal, isolation) directly to details in the source, and explains the resulting downward social drift (smaller flat, poorer area) with clear reference to the theory.
Secure: Identifies rejection and/or disengagement with some reference to the source, and links to social drift, though application may be partial.
Developing: Describes the theory in general terms with limited reference to Amir's specific situation.
Emerging: Names the theory or gives a basic, undeveloped point with little or no application to the source.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that schizophrenia is best explained by the biological explanation (dopamine hypothesis and brain dysfunction) rather than the psychological explanation (social drift theory). Refer to relevant research studies in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument that explains both explanations accurately, evaluates each with developed points (including strengths and criticisms such as the nature/nurture debate and the cause-and-effect problem), draws on the Daniel et al (1991) study or other evidence, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Explains both explanations with reasonable detail, offers some evaluation points, and attempts a judgement, though development may be uneven.
Developing: Describes one or both explanations with limited evaluation; judgement is weak, one-sided or missing.
Emerging: Basic, undeveloped description of one explanation only, with no meaningful evaluation or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which dispositional factor is most closely linked to obedience?
A) Self-esteem
B) Locus of control
C) Authoritarian personality
D) Deindividuation
practice_questions.marks: C) Authoritarian personality [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline how locus of control affects behaviour in a crowd.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying internal or external locus of control; one mark for a developed point about its effect (for example, internal locus of control makes a person more likely to resist joining antisocial crowd behaviour because they feel personally responsible for their own actions).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of self-esteem in conformity.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for stating that self-esteem affects conformity (e.g. low self-esteem increases conformity); one mark for a developed reason (e.g. low self-esteem leads to doubt in one's own judgement, so the person looks to the majority for reassurance); one mark for accurate use of specialist vocabulary or reference to hippocampal volume.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the authoritarian personality can lead to higher levels of obedience.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to two marks for identifying features of the authoritarian personality (rigid adherence to conventional values, strong respect for authority, intolerance of ambiguity); up to two further marks for explaining how this leads to obedience (e.g. challenging authority conflicts with the person's core values, so they obey orders without question even if harmful).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Read the source below, then answer the question.
Source: During a protest, most of the crowd around Jian begin vandalising a shop window. Jian refuses to join in. Afterwards he says he felt strongly that damaging property was wrong, no matter what everyone else around him was doing.
Using your knowledge of dispositional factors, explain why Jian did not join in with the antisocial crowd behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Marks for naming a relevant dispositional factor (morality and/or internal locus of control) AND linking it explicitly to the source. For example: Jian shows strong personal morality, believing damaging property is wrong regardless of the crowd's behaviour (up to 2-3 marks); Jian's statement that this held true "no matter what everyone else was doing" also suggests an internal locus of control, as he takes personal responsibility for his own actions rather than following the crowd's lead (up to 2-3 marks). Maximum 5 marks for full application to the specific source detail.
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that dispositional factors, rather than situational factors, are the main explanation for why people behave antisocially in crowds. Use your knowledge of research such as NatCen (2011) to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument drawing on both dispositional (self-esteem, locus of control, morality, authoritarian personality) and situational factors, applies NatCen (2011) accurately as evidence, evaluates issues such as generalisability, and reaches a clear, well-supported judgement.
Secure: Clear argument covering both dispositional and situational factors with relevant evidence including NatCen (2011); some evaluation and a supported conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points about dispositional factors with limited situational comparison; evaluation is basic or one-sided; NatCen (2011) may be named but not applied.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about crowd behaviour; little or no evaluation; no reference to research.

practice_questions.text: Which one of the following best describes confabulation?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: producing a false memory by filling a gap with invented but plausible detail, without intending to deceive. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the term used for a question phrased so that it suggests a particular answer and can distort memory.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for 'leading question' (accept close equivalent wording).

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by a 'schema' in the Theory of Reconstructive Memory.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying schema as a mental framework of knowledge/expectations from past experience; 1 further mark for stating it is used to interpret or fill gaps in new information. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how leading questions can cause distortion in eyewitness memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear, developed explanation linking specific wording of a leading question to a schema-consistent change in the memory, using correct terminology throughout.
Secure: Explains that leading questions suggest an answer which alters recall, with a relevant example.
Developing: Basic point that leading questions can change memory, with limited explanation of how.
Emerging: Vague or unsupported reference to questions affecting memory.

practice_questions.text: A witness to a robbery is later asked by police: 'How badly was the shop owner injured when the robber attacked him?' Using your knowledge of reconstructive memory, explain how this question might distort the witness's memory of the event.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names distortion and/or leading question, explicitly links the specific wording ('attacked', 'injured') in the source to a plausible change in the witness's schema-driven recall, and explains the likely direction of the distortion.
Secure: Identifies the question as leading and explains in general terms that it could distort the witness's memory of the event.
Developing: States the question could affect memory but does not link this clearly to the wording given in the source.
Emerging: Generic comment about memory being unreliable, with no application to the source.

practice_questions.text: 'Reconstructive memory theory shows that eyewitness testimony can never be trusted in court.' Evaluate this statement, using your knowledge of schemas, confabulation, distortion, leading questions and relevant research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument drawing on schemas, confabulation, distortion, leading questions and Braun, Ellis and Loftus (2002), with each evaluation point elaborated (e.g. reductionism/holism debate, self-report limitations) and a clear supported judgement on the statement.
Secure: Clear argument covering most key concepts and the named study, with some development of evaluation points and a stated judgement, though not fully balanced.
Developing: Some relevant description of the theory and/or study with limited evaluation; judgement is asserted rather than justified.
Emerging: Brief or partial description with little evaluation and no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which brain system did Eysenck link to low cortical arousal in extraverts?
A) The limbic system
B) The reticular activation system
C) The autonomic nervous system
D) The hippocampus
practice_questions.marks: B) The reticular activation system [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'psychoticism' in Eysenck's theory.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying psychoticism as a personality trait linked to aggression, low empathy or impulsivity; 1 mark for linking it to high testosterone (and low serotonin) or to antisocial behaviour. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Eysenck explained neuroticism using the autonomic nervous system and limbic system.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks for a developed description: 1 mark for stating the ANS reacts too strongly or quickly to stress; 1 mark for stating the limbic system amplifies emotional responses such as fear or anxiety; 1 mark for linking this to difficulty with self-control under pressure. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how difficulties in conditioning might make an extraverted child more likely to offend, according to Eysenck's theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that extraverts have chronically low arousal, so the anxiety response that pairs punishment with wrongdoing is weaker; therefore normal socialisation is less effective, leaving weaker learned restraint against rule-breaking, fully linked to increased offending risk.
Secure: Explains that extraverts condition less easily to punishment, so are less likely to learn to avoid antisocial behaviour, with some link to offending.
Developing: States extraverts don't condition as well but explanation of why, or the link to offending, is limited.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped point with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: A researcher is studying a group of teenagers with high psychoticism scores who show little remorse after breaking school rules. Using Eysenck's theory, explain why these teenagers might behave this way and suggest one criticism of using personality alone to explain their behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explicitly applies the scenario — names psychoticism and high testosterone, links this directly to the low empathy and rule-breaking described, then gives a developed criticism (e.g. individual differences or reductionism) referencing the specific group.
Secure: Names psychoticism and gives a biological link with some reference to the scenario; states a relevant criticism.
Developing: General theory knowledge given with limited link to the scenario; criticism is basic or missing.
Emerging: Minimal application; theory and scenario largely disconnected.

practice_questions.text: "Eysenck's Criminal Personality Theory is the best psychological explanation of why people commit crime." Discuss this statement, using your knowledge of Eysenck's theory, relevant research and at least one other explanation of criminal behaviour that you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument that explains Eysenck's PEN model and its biological basis, evaluates using Heaven (1996) and named criticisms (individual differences, reductionism, nature/nurture), compares against at least one other explanation (e.g. Social Learning Theory), and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of Eysenck's theory with relevant evidence and some evaluation; comparison with another explanation present but less developed; judgement given.
Developing: Mostly descriptive account of the theory with limited evaluation; comparison or judgement is basic or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about the theory; little to no evaluation or comparison; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of experiment takes place in a real-world setting where the researcher deliberately manipulates the independent variable, but participants remain in their natural environment?
A) Laboratory experiment
B) Field experiment
C) Natural experiment
D) Case study
practice_questions.marks: B) Field experiment [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one difference between an overt observation and a covert observation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid difference, for example: in an overt observation participants know they are being watched (and have given consent), whereas in a covert observation they do not know they are being watched (no consent given).

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by a structured interview.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks available:
• 1 mark for stating the interview uses a fixed, pre-decided set of questions asked in the same order to every participant.
• 1 mark for adding that this makes the interview easy to replicate and allows answers to be compared across participants.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between closed questions and open questions in a questionnaire.
practice_questions.marks:
3 marks available:
• 1 mark for stating closed questions offer a fixed set of possible answers, producing quantitative data.
• 1 mark for stating open questions have no fixed answers and let participants respond in their own words, producing qualitative data.
• 1 mark for a developed comparison, e.g. closed questions are quicker to analyse and compare, but open questions give richer, more detailed answers.

practice_questions.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using covert observation to study behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains both a strength and a weakness of covert observation with clear reasoning linking each to validity or ethics, e.g. participants behave naturally because they are unaware, increasing validity, but the lack of informed consent raises ethical concerns.
Secure: Identifies and explains one strength and one weakness with some development.
Developing: States a strength and a weakness with limited explanation.
Emerging: Names a strength or weakness with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to study how children play in a school playground without changing their natural behaviour. Using this information, suggest the most appropriate type of observation and explain why it is suitable for this scenario.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies a naturalistic, covert, non-participant observation as suitable and applies this precisely to the scenario, explaining how each feature (natural setting, unawareness, no researcher involvement) preserves natural behaviour.
Secure: Identifies a suitable observation type and links it to the scenario with clear explanation.
Developing: Identifies a relevant observation type with limited application to the scenario.
Emerging: Names an observation method with little or no link to the scenario.

practice_questions.text:
Which part of the brain generates random bursts of electrical activity during REM sleep, according to activation synthesis theory?
A) Cerebral cortex
B) Pons
C) Hippocampus
D) Hypothalamus
practice_questions.marks: B) Pons [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the brain structure that organises random neural signals into a dream narrative, according to activation synthesis theory.
practice_questions.marks: Cerebral cortex (accept cortex) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'synthesis' in the activation synthesis theory of dreaming.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that the cerebral cortex organises/interprets random neural signals; 1 mark for explaining this produces a story-like dream narrative. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how activity in the pons and limbic system during REM sleep contributes to the bizarre and emotional content of dreams.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains a clear causal chain linking random pons activity to bizarre cortical synthesis AND limbic system activity to emotional intensity, using accurate terminology throughout.
Secure: Explains both the pons's role in randomness and the limbic system's role in emotion, with mostly accurate terminology.
Developing: Describes the pons or limbic system's role but explanation of cause and effect is limited or one-sided.
Emerging: Basic, undeveloped reference to the brain and dreaming with little accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: A participant is woken during a period of REM sleep in a sleep laboratory. She reports a dream in which her school suddenly turns into a supermarket, her teacher's face keeps changing, and she feels intense fear throughout, even though nothing dangerous actually happens. Using activation synthesis theory, explain this participant's dream experience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Applies the theory precisely to the source — links random pons signals to the sudden scene/face changes (bizarreness), and limbic system activity to the intense fear, referencing the cortex's synthesis role, with clear reference to details from the source.
Secure: Applies most elements of the theory (pons, limbic system, cortex) to the source with some specific reference to source details.
Developing: Applies some theory terminology to the source but link to specific source detail is limited.
Emerging: General theory knowledge given with little or no application to the source.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the activation synthesis theory of dreaming. Use evidence from research to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument covering the theory's biological explanation (pons, limbic system, cortical synthesis), supported by Williams et al. (1992) evidence, with elaborated evaluation (e.g. reductionism/holism debate, comparison with Freud's theory) and a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Clear description of the theory and supporting study, with some developed evaluation points and a judgement, though not fully sustained throughout.
Developing: Some accurate description of the theory with limited evaluation; judgement may be brief or unsupported.
Emerging: Basic or fragmented points about dreaming with little use of the named theory, study or evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes sleep maintenance insomnia?
A) Difficulty falling asleep at the start of the night
B) Difficulty staying asleep, with frequent waking during the night
C) Sleeping for too many hours each night
D) A disorder only caused by hypothalamic damage
practice_questions.marks: B) Difficulty staying asleep, with frequent waking during the night [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the brain structure that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle and can cause insomnia if damaged.
practice_questions.marks: Hypothalamus [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline how sympathetic nervous system activity can contribute to sleep onset insomnia.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that the sympathetic nervous system triggers a fight-or-flight state; one mark for linking this to raised heart rate/alertness delaying sleep onset. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sleep clinic recorded the number of night-time wakings for seven insomnia patients over one night: 2, 4, 3, 8, 3, 3, 5. Calculate the mode number of wakings and state what this measure shows about the patients' sleep.
practice_questions.marks: Mode = 3 [1 mark]. Explanation that the mode shows the most frequently occurring number of wakings among the patients [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how relaxation techniques can be used to treat sleep onset insomnia, referring to the nervous system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed explanation, for example:
• Relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation or controlled breathing reduce sympathetic nervous system activity (1 mark)
• This lowers heart rate, muscle tension and mental alertness, reducing physiological arousal (1 mark)
• Reduced arousal allows the parasympathetic nervous system to dominate, creating physical calm (1 mark)
• This directly targets the hyperarousal that causes sleep onset insomnia, making it easier to fall asleep (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Discuss how effective relaxation techniques and sleep hygiene are as treatments for insomnia. In your answer, refer to the role of the nervous system and the physical environment, and reach a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, sustained argument that explains both relaxation techniques (nervous system arousal) and sleep hygiene (physical environment) with elaborated evaluation of strengths and limitations of each, reaching a clear, well-supported judgement about which is more effective or whether both are needed depending on cause.
Secure: Clear explanation of both treatments with relevant evaluation points (e.g. relaxation techniques may not help environment-caused insomnia; sleep hygiene may not help stress-caused insomnia) and a stated judgement.
Developing: Some explanation of one or both treatments with limited or undeveloped evaluation; judgement may be weak or unsupported.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about insomnia treatments with little or no evaluation and no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best explains why a jingle in a television advert helps a customer recall the product later in a shop?
A) It reduces the price of the product
B) It acts as a retrieval cue that triggers the stored memory
C) It prevents the advert from being shown again
D) It removes the need for repetition
practice_questions.marks: B) It acts as a retrieval cue that triggers the stored memory [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique, other than repetition, that advertisers use to improve customers' recall of a product.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: use of cues (e.g. a logo, jingle or slogan); avoiding overload; autobiographical advertising. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'avoiding overload' as a technique used in advertising.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: recognising that short-term memory has a limited capacity.
1 mark: explaining that adverts limit the amount of information shown at once so it is not lost before it can be rehearsed/stored. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how repetition can help move information from short-term memory into long-term memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear, developed description linking repeated exposure to increased rehearsal and successful transfer to long-term storage, using correct terminology (e.g. multi-store model, rehearsal).
Secure: Accurate description of repetition increasing rehearsal, with a link to long-term memory transfer.
Developing: Basic description of repetition with limited link to memory transfer.
Emerging: Simple or vague statement about repeating adverts. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the findings of Braun, Ellis and Loftus (2002) support the use of autobiographical advertising as a recall technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the study showed nostalgic, personal imagery in adverts could shape or distort participants' memories of a product experience, and links this clearly to reconstructive memory theory (schemas, confabulation) as the mechanism.
Secure: Explains the study's finding about advertising shaping personal memories with some link to reconstructive memory.
Developing: States a basic finding from the study with limited explanation of why it works.
Emerging: Vague or inaccurate reference to the study. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A cereal brand's television advert features a jingle repeated three times, a bright red logo shown in every scene, and a voiceover asking viewers to picture eating breakfast with their family as a child. Using the source, explain two techniques the advert uses to improve consumers' recall of the product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two techniques from the source (e.g. repetition of the jingle; cue of the red logo; autobiographical advertising via the childhood scene) and explains, with explicit reference to the source detail, how each improves recall.
Secure: Identifies two techniques and links each to a source detail, with some explanation of the memory process involved.
Developing: Identifies one or two techniques with limited or generic reference to the source.
Emerging: Describes the advert without applying named memory techniques. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes minority influence?
A) A large group pressuring an individual to conform immediately
B) A small group whose consistent, confident message gradually changes majority opinion
C) An individual obeying a legitimate authority figure
D) A crowd losing its sense of individual identity
practice_questions.marks: B) A small group whose consistent, confident message gradually changes majority opinion [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one process that explains why people go along with majority influence.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for either: normative social influence (wanting to be liked/accepted) OR informational social influence (believing the majority has better information). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline how consistency helps a minority group achieve social change.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the minority repeats the same message over time and agrees with each other (consistency); 1 mark for developing that this makes the majority take the message seriously and reconsider their own view rather than dismissing it.

practice_questions.text: Explain how majority influence can help to reduce stigma around mental health problems.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for developed explanatory points such as: once a large proportion of people openly discuss mental health, individuals feel normative pressure to accept this as the norm too (1-2 marks); individuals may also assume the majority holds accurate information about mental health and adjust their own attitude to match, i.e. informational social influence (1-2 marks); credit reference to how this reduces stigma/discrimination by making open discussion the accepted behaviour rather than something to hide (1-2 marks).

practice_questions.text: A school council introduces a weekly assembly where students who have experienced mental health problems share their story. At first, most students do not join in, but after a year, most students in the school openly discuss mental health and support the assembly. Using the source, apply your knowledge of minority and majority influence to explain how attitudes in the school changed.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks: 1-2 marks for identifying the students sharing stories as a consistent minority whose message did not change over the year, linked to the source; 1-2 marks for explaining that once most students in the school supported the assembly, remaining students felt normative/informational pressure to conform to this new majority view, linked to the source; 1 mark for a concluding link showing how minority influence started the change and majority influence sustained or spread it across the whole school.

practice_questions.text: "Minority influence is more effective than majority influence at creating lasting change in attitudes towards mental health." Evaluate this statement, using your knowledge of minority influence, majority influence and mental health stigma.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument that explains both minority and majority influence in detail, applies them accurately to mental health stigma, develops multiple evaluation points (e.g. internalisation vs compliance, speed of change vs depth of change) and reaches a clear, well-supported judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of both minority and majority influence with relevant application to mental health stigma; some evaluation points made and developed; a judgement is reached but may be less fully supported.
Developing: Explains minority and/or majority influence with limited application to mental health; evaluation is basic or one-sided; judgement is present but undeveloped.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about minority or majority influence; little or no application to mental health stigma; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the aim of restorative justice?
A) To remove the offender from society for as long as possible
B) To bring the offender face-to-face with the victim so they understand the impact of their crime
C) To fine the offender the maximum amount possible
D) To identify the offender's personality type
