practice_questions.marks: B) To bring the offender face-to-face with the victim so they understand the impact of their crime [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of community sentence an offender might receive instead of prison.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any one of the following:
• Unpaid work / community payback
• Curfew (e.g. electronic tagging)
• A treatment or rehabilitation programme
[1 mark for any one correct answer]

practice_questions.text: Describe how positive role models are used as part of rehabilitation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly describes offenders being exposed to models showing pro-social behaviour (e.g. mentors, reformed ex-offenders) and links this to learning behaviour through observation and imitation, using accurate terminology.
Secure: Describes the use of positive role models in rehabilitation with some relevant, accurate detail.
Developing: Basic description of role models with limited detail or some inaccuracy.
Emerging: A simple, undeveloped point about role models.

practice_questions.text: Explain why prisons might not always reduce reoffending.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives two developed explanatory points (e.g. contact with other offenders can act as criminal role models increasing imitation; limited access to rehabilitation programmes means underlying causes of offending are not addressed) with clear cause-and-effect reasoning.
Secure: Gives one developed explanatory point or two under-developed points about why prisons may not reduce reoffending.
Developing: Identifies a relevant point with limited explanation of why it affects reoffending.
Emerging: A simple, undeveloped point with little explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Read the source below, then answer the question that follows.

Jake was convicted of a minor theft. Instead of being sent to prison, the court gave him a community sentence: 100 hours of unpaid work and a six-month curfew monitored by an electronic tag.

Using the source, explain two advantages of giving Jake a community sentence rather than a prison sentence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two advantages and links each explicitly to details in the source (e.g. Jake can keep working and stay connected to family while completing his unpaid work; the curfew and tag allow monitoring without removing him from the community), with clear application.
Secure: Identifies two advantages with some reference to the source, though application may be less explicit.
Developing: Identifies one advantage with reference to the source, or two advantages with generic, unlinked reasoning.
Emerging: States a general advantage of community sentences without applying it to Jake's situation.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether rehabilitation is more effective than punishment at reducing criminal and anti-social behaviour. In your answer, you should consider restorative justice, positive role models, prisons, community sentences and fines, and reach a supported conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument covering rehabilitation and punishment approaches with sustained, elaborated evaluation of each (each point developed with a clear reason) and a well-supported judgement that draws on relevant theory (e.g. Social Learning Theory, the nature/nurture or free will/determinism debate) from across the course.
Secure: Clear argument covering most named approaches with relevant evaluation and a supported conclusion, though not all points are fully elaborated or synoptic links are limited.
Developing: Some description of relevant approaches with basic evaluation; conclusion may be asserted rather than supported by reasoning.
Emerging: Simple, mostly descriptive points about punishment and/or rehabilitation with little evaluation and no clear conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a case study?
A) A method that tests many people using a written survey
B) An in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event
C) A method that always establishes cause and effect
D) A statistical technique that measures association between variables
practice_questions.marks: B) An in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A researcher uses hospital records that were originally collected for a different purpose by hospital staff. Identify whether this is primary or secondary data.
practice_questions.marks: Secondary data [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A study found the correlation between hours of sleep and reaction time to be −0.72. A different study found the correlation between hours of revision and exam score to be +0.65. Calculate the difference between the strength of these two correlations, ignoring their direction, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: 0.72 − 0.65 = 0.07 [1 mark for correctly subtracting the values ignoring the sign; 1 mark for the correct final answer of 0.07] [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using case studies in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly describes one strength (e.g. rich in-depth qualitative data on a rare or unusual case) and one weakness (e.g. a small sample limits generalisability) using accurate terminology.
Secure: Describes one strength and one weakness with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Identifies a strength and/or weakness but with limited description.
Emerging: Vague or absent reference to strengths or weaknesses of case studies.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a correlation cannot be used to prove that one variable causes another. Use the term 'third variable' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains clearly that neither variable is manipulated so a causal link cannot be established, and explains the third variable problem with a plausible example.
Secure: States that correlation does not show causation and gives some explanation of the third variable problem.
Developing: States that correlation cannot prove causation but the explanation of why, or the third variable idea, is only named rather than explained.
Emerging: Simple assertion with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to study whether the number of hours teenagers spend on social media is related to their reported levels of anxiety. She asks 60 teenagers to complete a questionnaire recording their weekly social media use (in hours) and their anxiety score (out of 50). Using the source, identify the type of data collected and explain how the researcher could display and interpret the relationship between the two variables.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies the data as quantitative (numerical hours and scores), explains the researcher could use a scatter diagram, and correctly links this to the source, e.g. identifying it would show a positive correlation if anxiety rises with social media use.
Secure: Identifies quantitative data and describes a scatter diagram with some reference to the source.
Developing: Identifies the data type or method of display but with limited application to the specific source.
Emerging: Vague or generic answer with little reference to the study described.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Piaget's concept of readiness in education?
A) A child should be taught anything as soon as they are old enough
B) A child should only be taught new content once they have reached the stage of thinking needed to understand it
C) A child's readiness depends only on their IQ score
D) A child is 'ready' once they can memorise facts
practice_questions.marks: B) A child should only be taught new content once they have reached the stage of thinking needed to understand it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the term used by Dweck to describe the belief that ability can be developed through effort and practice.
practice_questions.marks: Growth mindset. [1 mark for correct term]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'active learning' in Piaget's application to education.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying learning through direct, hands-on interaction with real objects/activities; one further mark for explaining that this is preferred over passive listening because children build understanding through activity. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Willingham's research on learning styles has changed the way teachers plan lessons.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains clearly that research does not support matching teaching to a preferred learning style, and links this to teaching through meaning, with a developed example.
Secure: Explains that learning styles are not supported by research and describes teaching through meaning with some development.
Developing: States that learning styles have been challenged and briefly mentions teaching through meaning, with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple or partial point with little development.

practice_questions.text: A Year 3 teacher (pupils aged 7 to 8) is planning a maths lesson on fractions. She gives each pupil a set of physical counters to divide into groups, rather than starting with a written worksheet of fraction sums. Using your knowledge of Piaget's application to education, explain why this approach suits pupils of this age.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names the concrete operational stage (ages 7 to 11) and active learning, linking both explicitly to the scenario — explaining that pupils at this stage learn best through hands-on interaction with real objects rather than abstract written problems, with clear application to the counters.
Secure: Identifies active learning and/or the concrete operational stage and links this to the scenario with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a relevant concept but application to the specific scenario is limited.
Emerging: Simple or generic point with little or no application to the scenario.

practice_questions.text: 'Piaget's theory of cognitive development has been more useful for improving education than the learning theories of Dweck and Willingham.' Discuss this statement, drawing on your knowledge of Piaget's application to education and the application of growth mindset and teaching-through-meaning research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument that draws on Piaget's application (readiness, key stages, active learning, intelligence) and the learning theories (growth mindset, teaching through meaning), with sustained, elaborated evaluation of each and a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Clear argument covering both Piaget's and the learning theories' applications with relevant evaluation, reaching a judgement, though development may be less consistent.
Developing: Some relevant description of Piaget and/or the learning theories with limited evaluation; judgement may be brief or unsupported.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points with little accurate application or evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a key idea of social rank theory?
A) Depression is caused by an overactive dopamine system
B) Depression is caused by watching violent video games
C) Depression may serve an evolutionary function by reducing conflict after a loss in social rank
D) Depression is caused entirely by irrational beliefs about activating events
practice_questions.marks: C) Depression may serve an evolutionary function by reducing conflict after a loss in social rank [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the name of the psychologist who developed the ABC model of clinical depression.
practice_questions.marks: Albert Ellis [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what social rank theory suggests happens to a person's behaviour after they experience a significant loss of social status.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying reduced activity/submissive, withdrawn behaviour; 1 mark for explaining this reduces the risk of further conflict with higher-ranking individuals. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how irrational beliefs about an activating event can lead to the consequences described in Ellis's ABC model. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names all three components (A, B, C), explains clearly that the belief (not the event) determines the consequence, and gives an accurate, relevant example.
Secure: Explains that beliefs cause consequences with a mostly accurate example, minor gaps in detail.
Developing: Basic reference to the ABC model with limited explanation or a vague example.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped point; model not clearly explained.

practice_questions.text: Priya was not invited to a friend's birthday party. She believes this means 'nobody likes me and I will always be alone.' She has since stopped going out and feels persistently low. Using the ABC model, explain how Priya's irrational beliefs may have contributed to her low mood.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies the activating event (not being invited), the irrational belief (overgeneralised, catastrophic interpretation), and the consequence (low mood, withdrawal), linking all three explicitly to Priya's situation.
Secure: Identifies most of A, B and C and links them reasonably well to the scenario.
Developing: Identifies at least one component of the model and makes a limited link to the scenario.
Emerging: Very limited reference to the model or the scenario.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that clinical depression is better explained by biological factors (social rank theory) than by psychological factors (the ABC model). Refer to psychological theories and at least one core study in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument covering both social rank theory and the ABC model, with sustained, elaborated evaluation (each point given a developed reason) drawing on the Tandoc et al. (2015) study and the reductionism/holism and freewill/determinism debates, reaching a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Clear coverage of both theories with relevant evaluation and some use of the core study, reaching a judgement with some support.
Developing: Some description of both theories but evaluation is limited, undeveloped, or one-sided; weak or missing judgement.
Emerging: Mostly descriptive; little or no evaluation; no clear judgement reached.

practice_questions.text:
Which neurotransmitter do anti-psychotic drugs mainly target to reduce the symptoms of schizophrenia?
A) Serotonin
B) Dopamine
C) Adrenaline
D) GABA
practice_questions.marks: B) Dopamine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique used in neuropsychology to study the brain of a person with schizophrenia or clinical depression.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: brain imaging / scanning techniques; neuropsychological tests (e.g. the Wechsler Memory Scale) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline how anti-depressant medication improves the mental health of a person with clinical depression.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies that anti-depressants increase the availability of serotonin at the synapse (e.g. by blocking reuptake).
1 mark: links this to an improvement in mood/reduction in depressive symptoms.
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which psychotherapy can improve the mental health of a person with clinical depression.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per developed point (max 4). Accept, for example: (1) helps the person identify and challenge negative/irrational thought patterns, reducing the beliefs that maintain low mood; (2) gradually rebuilds activities/relationships the person has withdrawn from, giving them coping skills they can continue to use after therapy ends.

practice_questions.text: Read the following extract: 'Aisha has been diagnosed with clinical depression. Her doctor has prescribed her a course of anti-depressants and referred her for psychotherapy sessions with a clinical psychologist.' Using your knowledge of the development of treatments for clinical depression, explain how each of the two interventions named in the source might improve Aisha's mental health.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks. Award marks for: explanation of anti-depressants linked to increased serotonin availability at the synapse and improved mood, explicitly applied to Aisha (up to 2-3 marks); explanation of psychotherapy linked to changing negative thought/behaviour patterns, explicitly applied to Aisha (up to 2-3 marks). Full marks require explicit reference to the source, not generic textbook knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of biological and psychological treatments in improving the mental health of people with schizophrenia and/or clinical depression. In your answer, refer to how neuropsychology has contributed to understanding these treatments.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced essay covering biological treatments (anti-psychotics/anti-depressants and their neural mechanisms) and psychological treatments (psychotherapy), with sustained, elaborated evaluation of strengths and limitations of each, explicit reference to neuropsychology, and a clear, well-supported judgement.
Secure: Clear coverage of both biological and psychological treatments with relevant evaluation and some reference to neuropsychology, reaching a supported conclusion, though evaluation may be less consistently developed.
Developing: Some description of treatments with limited evaluation; points may be listed rather than developed, and neuropsychology may be mentioned only briefly or omitted.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about treatment with little or no evaluation and no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher records the number of hours slept by 10 participants each night for a week. Which graph would be most appropriate for showing how the group's average sleep changed across the seven days?
A) Pie chart
B) Line graph
C) Bar chart
D) Scatter diagram
practice_questions.marks: B) Line graph [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A memory test is given to six participants, who recall the following numbers of words: 6, 8, 8, 10, 12, 14. Calculate the mean number of words recalled, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working (6+8+8+10+12+14 = 58, then 58 divided by 6). 1 mark for the correct final answer: 9.67 (to 2 decimal places) or an equivalent correctly rounded value. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the modal class in a set of grouped data.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise, developed description using correct terminology — names the modal class as the group/class interval with the highest frequency and explains why the term 'modal class' rather than 'mode' is used for grouped data. Secure: Clear description identifying the modal class as the group with the highest frequency. Developing: Basic description with some inaccuracy or vagueness. Emerging: Attempts a description but shows limited understanding. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A researcher measures the same group of participants' anxiety levels using the same questionnaire on two separate occasions, one month apart, and finds very similar scores both times. Explain what this tells us about the external reliability of the questionnaire.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that similar scores across the two occasions show high external reliability because the measure produces consistent results over time, linking this to the test-retest method in the scenario. Secure: Explains that consistent scores over time indicate reliability, with some link to external reliability specifically. Developing: States that the questionnaire is reliable without explaining the reasoning fully. Emerging: Identifies reliability as relevant but gives little or no explanation. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A psychologist observed children's play behaviour in a school playground and asked a second, independent observer to code the same behaviour using the same checklist. Using this source, explain how the psychologist could check the inter-rater reliability of the observation, and suggest what a low level of agreement between the two observers would mean for the study.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Applies the concept precisely to the source, explaining that inter-rater reliability is checked by comparing the level of agreement between the two observers' codings of the same behaviour, and explains that low agreement would suggest the observation is unreliable/subjective and the results cannot be trusted. Secure: Applies inter-rater reliability to the source with a clear but less developed explanation of what low agreement would mean. Developing: Some reference to the source with generic reliability knowledge; limited application. Emerging: Generic reliability point with little or no reference to the source. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Descriptive statistics and checks of reliability and validity are equally important when judging the value of psychological research.' Discuss this statement, drawing on your knowledge of measures of central tendency, reliability and validity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument drawing on descriptive statistics (mean/median/mode/range) and both reliability (internal/external/inter-rater) and validity (ecological/population/construct), with each point elaborated with a developed reason and a clear supported judgement reached at the end. Secure: Clear argument covering statistics and reliability/validity with some evaluation and a judgement, though development may be uneven. Developing: Mostly descriptive account of statistics and/or reliability/validity with limited evaluation or an unsupported judgement. Emerging: Basic or partial points with little synthesis and no clear judgement. [13 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A participant in a memory experiment notices the researcher's tone becomes warmer when they give a correct answer, and starts trying harder to please the researcher. This is best described as:
A) Observer bias
B) Social desirability bias
C) Demand characteristics
D) Cultural bias
practice_questions.marks: C) Demand characteristics [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between experimenter bias and observer bias.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each accurate point (max 2):
• Experimenter bias is when a researcher's expectations unconsciously affect how they run a study or interact with participants.
• Observer bias is when an observer's expectations affect what behaviour they notice or record during an observation.
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe how age bias could affect the conclusions drawn from a study into memory decline that only samples participants aged 65 to 75.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly describes that the narrow age sample means findings may not apply to younger or much older people, with a specific consequence for the conclusion drawn.
Secure: Describes that results from one age group may be wrongly generalised to all ages, with some explanation.
Developing: States that age bias is present but the description is vague or lacks a clear consequence.
Emerging: Names age bias only, with no description.

practice_questions.text: A researcher who strongly believes that violent video games cause aggression conducts an observation of children's play, coding ambiguous shoving as 'aggressive'. Explain how this could lead to biased results, referring to both observer bias and experimenter bias.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains observer bias (the researcher's prior belief leads them to interpret ambiguous behaviour as aggressive, inflating the aggression score) and experimenter bias (the researcher's expectations could subtly affect how they set up or run the observation), each with a clear causal link to biased results.
Secure: Explains one of the two biases clearly and makes a basic reference to the other.
Developing: Names both biases but explanation of cause and effect is limited.
Emerging: Describes the scenario without explaining either bias.

practice_questions.text: A questionnaire asks participants: 'Don't you agree that violent video games make children more aggressive?' Using this source, explain one way in which this question could produce biased data, and suggest one way the researcher could rewrite it to reduce that bias.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names bias in questioning specifically, explains clearly how the wording leads participants toward agreement (using the exact wording from the source), and gives a well-reworded, neutral alternative question.
Secure: Identifies bias in questioning and gives a workable rewritten question, with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies that the question is 'leading' or 'biased' without naming the specific type, and offers a limited rewrite.
Emerging: Describes the source without identifying the bias or offering a usable rewrite.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which bias is a serious problem for psychological research. In your answer, refer to at least two different types of bias (for example, demand characteristics, observer effect, social desirability, gender, cultural, age, experimenter, observer bias or bias in questioning) and to ways researchers can reduce bias when designing an investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument covering at least two named biases with developed evaluative points (strengths and weaknesses of each), clear reference to methods of reducing bias in study design, and a supported overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with at least two named biases, relevant evaluative points and some reference to reducing bias, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Some relevant points made but description dominates over evaluation; bias types may be named without being fully explained or linked to reducing bias.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points; bias types may be vague or missing; no clear judgement reached.
